panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Contrast-enhanced axial CT of the patient demonstrates the pleural empyema component of thoracic empyema necessitans, arrowed in the caption. B: Coronal CT shows the empyema with contiguous transpleural extension into the chest wall and left upper abdominal quadrant, matching the article’s diagnosis of Actinomyces meyeri empyema necessitatis.

panels.figure_caption: CT-scan of 61-year-old female showed a pleural empyema ( A : blue arrow, B : white arrow) with expansion per continuitatem to the left chest and left upper abdominal quadrant ( B : red arrow). CT, computed tomography.
in_text_mentions: workup included X-ray imaging of the chest and showed pleural effusion of the left side. Ultrasound of the swelling revealed a large abscess of the left chest with suspicion of communication to the pleural effusion. Following CT showed a pleural empyema with expansion per continuitatem to the left chest and left upper abdominal quadrant ( Fig. 3 ). Puncture of chest abscess formation revealed pus. Microbiological cultures returned positive for A. meyeri and Staphylococcus hominis . She was started on sulbactam and ampicillin and was urgently transferred to our hospital for further management.

plate_findings.evidence: fracture of the right sixth rib
extensive abscess through the right chest wall

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Axial chest CT at upper level demonstrating right sixth rib fracture and transpleural extension of empyema through the chest wall, characteristic of thoracic empyema necessitans. B: Axial chest CT at lower level showing pleural effusion and lower lobe opacities in the context of thoracic empyema necessitans.
panels.attribution_text: Ohki et al. Group B streptococcal empyema necessitatis with pleural fistula after blunt trauma: A case report.. International journal of surgery case reports 2019. doi:10.1016/j.ijscr.2019.09.006. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
in_text_mentions: ng. Laboratory data showed a white cell count of 13,800/mm3, a C-reactive protein level of 296 mg/l, a serum glucose level of 462 mg/dl, and a glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) concentration of 9.9%. Chest computed tomography (CT) scans on admission are shown in Fig. 1. These showed the fracture of the right sixth rib, a partially destroyed right middle lobe of the lung, and an extensive abscess through the right chest wall. Consolidation and ground-glass opacities in both lower lobes of the lungs suggestive of aspiration pneumonia were also noted.Fig. 1Chest computed tomography (CT) on day 1.Fig. 1

panels.rationale: Single-panel contrast-enhanced chest CT from a human patient with thoracic empyema necessitans, demonstrating classic CT manifestations of the disease: loculated pleural empyema with split pleura sign and transpleural extension into the left chest wall with surrounding fat stranding, consistent with the target disease described in the article title and caption, with no excluded content present.
panels.attribution_text: Gerlach et al. Empyema Necessitatis: A Rare Complication of Empyema.. Cureus 2023. doi:10.7759/cureus.48973. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 4.
panels.figure_caption: Chest CT on day 2 of admission, suspicious for loculated empyema.
in_text_mentions: .3 x 3.8 x 2.2 cm, approximately 3 mm beneath the skin, as shown in Figure 3. CT chest with contrast on day 2 of admission demonstrated an area of large loculation with central hypodensity containing a mixture of simple to more complex fluid with surrounding rim of enhancement in the left lower lobe, suspicious for a loculated empyema. CT also demonstrated a left lower anterior chest wall hypoenhancing ovoid structure measuring approximately 4.6 x 2.8 cm with associated fat stranding of the surrounding tissue and an additional, more inferior lesion measuring 2.8 x 1.5 cm, as shown in Figure 4.
